newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Bundesbank denies EMU report in gold feud.
newsitem.headline: German Bundesbank denies EMU report in gold feud.

text.p: The head of Germany's powerful Bundesbank, locked in a bitter battle with Bonn over gold and currency reserves, Sunday denied he had proposed a delay in the 1999 start date for Europe's single currency.
Hans Tietmeyer insisted he was committed to the European Union's Maastricht Treaty, which lays down the timetable and criteria for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
But he reiterated the Bundesbank's opposition to Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to revalue the bank's reserves this year and called on Bonn to take proper note of its objections.
Tietmeyer's statement aimed to dampen speculation he would rather sacrifice EMU than agree to Waigel's plan.

The speculation reached fever pitch after Der Spiegel magazine quoted Tietmeyer as breaking one of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's political taboos -- asking if Bonn and Paris could delay the start of the single currency.

Some members of Kohl's coalition also voiced opposition to Waigel's revaluation plan, raising the possibility that the veteran chancellor may not be able to muster a majority to push the controversial measure through parliament.
A related dispute over how to fill shortfalls in government finances, where Waigel is on collision course with the Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners, added to Kohl's woes.

Tietmeyer, a former Kohl protege, dismissed the Spiegel story. "Reports of suggestions by the Bundesbank or its president in favour of a postponement of the start of the monetary union are not accurate," he said in a statement.
"The Deutsche Bundesbank naturally stands by the Maastricht Treaty. The bank has already been working intensively for a long time on the preparation of monetary union with a stable euro."

The bank has condemned the gold plan as an attack on its fabled independence, but Waigel and other coalition leaders, turning the row into a battle between institutions, stressed that parliament was also an independent body.

"I expect the Bundesbank to respect the legislative independence of politics just as politics always respects the independence of the Bundesbank in monetary policy," Waigel said during a weekend bicycle tour in southern Germany.
Wolfgang Schaeuble, the parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), was even more blunt.

"The decision on the question we now face is to be taken by the legislature, whose independence is not less than that of the Bundesbank," Kohl's chief lieutenant wrote in a letter to his members of parliament to rally support for the plan.
A leading industry umbrella group said everyone was agreed the revaluation had to take place and the unresolved questions of when and how should be settled as quickly as possible.

"The timing and methods should be decided soon," said Hans Peter Stihl, the head of the German Chambers of Industry and Commerce. "A continuation of this confusing discussion unsettles industry and its planning."

Waigel's plan aims to reap 20 billion marks ($12 billion) that could partly ease Bonn's debt burden and help meet the EMU entry criteria. The decision on which countries qualify for the currency will be based on data for 1997.
Tietmeyer said the Bundesbank's main objection concerned the fact that the revaluation would boost 1997 balance sheets.
"The Bundesbank hopes that the German government and parliament will take appropriate consideration of these objections when they make their decisions," he said.
Grumbling from members of Kohl's coalition suggested several members of parliament were indeed taking heed.
FDP budget expert Juergen Koppelin urged Bonn to retreat from what is shaping up to be an unprecedented clash between the government and the central bank.
